steps.observation: You have 60 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The foghorn had been silent for three nights when Elias woke to the sound of knocking.

Three hollow raps, spaced like distant waves against rock.

He lay in the narrow cot beneath the spiral stair, listening. Wind slithered around the stone tower, a restless whisper. The sea, far below, answered with its slow, dark breathing. No more knocking.

Elias sat up. His back complained like old rope. “Storm coming,” he murmured, though the air felt too still.

He climbed the stairs, hand sliding over iron worn smooth by decades of his own touch and those who’d come before. The lantern room waited at the top, a glass crown ringed in salt scars. Somewhere in the ascent, the tower’s familiar chill eased; up here the great lamp kept a small, stubborn warmth.

He checked the clockwork first. Its brass heart ticked obediently, driving the lens in its endless rotation. The mantle’s flame burned steady within the crystal drum, gathering itself into a single white eye that swept the horizon each forty seconds.

His logbook, open on the desk by the window, recorded nothing unusual: wind east-northeast, visibility poor, one trawler at dusk.

He almost convinced himself he’d dreamed the sound when it came again—three raps, nearer now, from the cast-iron hatch that opened to the gallery outside.

No boat could tie up to the rocks below in this swell. The supply tender was a week away, and he’d long ago stopped expecting company that wasn’t scheduled, signed, and stamped by the Service.

For an instant, he thought of his father, the way the old man had stood in this very room, boots braced, spinning storms into stories.

“Some nights,” his father used to say, voice low as the surf, “the sea remembers who it’s taken and comes knocking for more.”

Elias snorted at his own memory and crossed to the hatch. The world beyond the glass was a smudged charcoal drawing: fog pressed close, swallowing the beam as soon as it left the lens, sea and sky the same colorless void.

He unlatched the hatch and pushed it open.

The gallery circled the tower like a narrow stone belt. It was empty. No gulls roosted along the rail. No lantern bobbed in the waves below. Only the sound of water clawing at the cliffs.

“Anyone there?” he called, feeling faintly foolish for raising his voice against so much nothing.

The third knock came not from the door this time, but from beneath his feet.

Elias froze. Below the gallery was only the tower wall and, beyond it, solid rock. And under that, the bone-white restlessness of the sea.

The knock repeated, dull and insistent, like fists on a buried coffin.

He shut the hatch slowly and descended, following the sound as it slid downward through stone. It led him past the sleeping quarters, the storeroom of paraffin and spare mantles, the cramped kitchen with its blackened kettle, down to the service level where the tower met the headland.

Here, the stone sweated even in winter. Moss bruised the mortar, and the air tasted of iron and old storms. A heavy door, seldom used, opened into a shallow cave the builders had carved when they anchored the foundation into the rock. He kept old buoys and cracked lenses here, glass riddled with fractures like frozen lightning.

The knocking was louder now. Three strikes, a pause, three more. It came from the sea-side wall.

Elias lifted the hooded lantern from its peg and let its glow smear over the rock. No cracks. No signs of settlement. Just slick granite flecked with mica.

“Old man,” he muttered to the memory of his father, “you told too many tales.”

The next knock shook fine grit from the ceiling.

He pressed his palm flat to the stone.

It was warm.

Not the wan warmth of his lantern, but something deeper, as if the rock remembered sun that hadn’t yet risen.

With each set of knocks, the warmth flared, then faded.

Elias swallowed. “Who’s there?” he asked the wall.

The reply, if it was one, came as a faint vibration against his hand, so soft he might have mistaken it for his pulse.

Help.

The word formed in his mind fully formed, as clear as if someone had spoken in his ear.

He jerked his hand back. His breath misted the lantern glass. No one else had a key to the tower. No radio call had come. The last entry in his log was his own, in the same thin, slanting hand he’d used for years.

Help.

Elias was not a man given to fancies, but he had lived most of his life in conversation with things that could not answer. You spoke to the flame when it guttered. To the lens when it collected fog like tears. To the sea when it pounded all night, asking nothing and giving less.

“Where?” he asked, feeling absurd.

Below.

He could have ignored it. No rule in the Service manual covered voices in stone. The correct procedure, if there was one, was likely to double-check the light, wind the clock, and blame the rest on isolation and the low, humming pressure of the weather.

Instead, Elias set the lantern on the floor and found the cold iron handle that controlled the storm drains. The tower’s base sat in a shallow groove that let rainwater and spray escape back to the sea through a narrow channel. Over time, debris and weed choked it. Old keepers, his father included, had enlarged a section of it into a crawlspace—a foolish, dangerous thing, and strictly against regulations.

His father had shown it to him once, when he was twelve and still thought the world ended at the red-buoy line.

“A bolt-hole,” his father had said. “For when the sea comes higher than it should.”

Elias had never used it. Never needed to.

Now, as he hauled the handle up and the rusted mechanism protested, the knocking pulsed through the stone like a heartbeat.

The opening revealed itself in a low, dark maw at the base of the wall, barely wide enough for him to squeeze through. Black water lapped just beyond, surging with each distant wave. The smell was rank with kelp and something older.

He should have shut it again. He thought of the logbook upstairs, its rows of obedient entries. The Service would ask why he’d left his post. The light must never go out.

He listened.

Help.

It was thin now, almost drowned by the gurgle of the drains.

“I’m coming,” Elias said, and the word felt strange in his mouth, as if he were stepping into one of his father’s stories against his will.

He slid on his back into the gap, boots first, holding the lantern out before him. Rock scraped his shoulders. Cold water soaked his clothes. For a moment, panic caught his chest like a hook—he had the absurd conviction that the sea would jam itself into the opening and pin him there forever.

But then he was through, into a low tunnel running along the cliffside, half-filled with water that surged and hissed with each oscillation of the tide. The lantern’s light painted jagged patterns on the ceiling.

Ahead, the passage bent, then opened out near a fractured section where storm and time had chewed at the rock. Through a broken lip he could see open air and, far below, the froth of waves.

A shape clung to the outer ledge.

For a dizzy second, he thought it was just wreckage—a tangle of rope and oilskins. Then it moved, feebly, a hand lifting and slipping, fingers clawing at algae-slick stone.

“Hold fast!” he shouted, though the wind likely tore his voice to shreds.

He wedged the lantern into a dry niche and wriggled closer until he could reach an arm through the gap. Spray slapped his face. The drop below was a hungry darkness.

“Take my hand!”

Cold fingers latched onto his wrist with a strength born of terror. He braced his shoulders against the tunnel walls and pulled. The ledge outside offered no purchase for his feet, only slime and the endless draw of the sea. His arms trembled. Once, his grip faltered, and the weight on his wrist lurched away, dragging his shoulder hard against the rock.

“Don’t let go,” he hissed, more to himself than to the stranger.

With a final heave, the figure slid through the gap and collapsed half on top of him in the tunnel. They lay panting in the darkness, salted water pooling around them.

The stranger was younger than Elias by decades, face pale beneath streaks of blood and seawater. A tattered lifejacket hung open at his chest. His eyes, when they found Elias’s, were wild and bright.

“The light,” the young man gasped. “I saw—the light—I thought—”

“It’s burning,” Elias said. “You hit the reef?”

“Boat went to pieces. Thought I was done.” His voice broke into a ragged laugh that sounded close to sobbing. “Then the rock started…knocking.”

Elias stared at him.

“Felt it through the water,” the survivor muttered, eyes already sagging closed. “Like someone was…calling. Then I saw the light, and—”

He slipped into unconsciousness.

The tunnel shuddered as a wave struck the cliff outside, sending a tongue of black water snaking past their boots.

Elias, heart pounding, dragged the young man back the way he’d come, inch by awkward inch, until the two of them spilled into the service level of the tower.

By the time he got the survivor to the cot under the spiral stairs and stripped off the worst of his sodden clothing, the flame in the lantern room had started to gutter. The clockwork, unchecked, had slowed.

Elias climbed, legs burning, and trimmed the mantle, righted the weight chain, and sent the great lens turning again. The beam swept out into the fog, bright and steady, indifferent to the drama at its feet.

Only then, leaning on the brass rail, did Elias let himself breathe.

The sea was still invisible. Somewhere out there, floating in that blind gray, might be more wreckage, more survivors. He would radio the coastguard when the generator stopped sulking and agreed to carry more than a dim mutter.

Behind him, the tower stones ticked as they yielded their warmth back to the surrounding cold.

“Thank you,” Elias said in a low voice, and he wasn’t entirely sure whether he spoke to the flame, the rock, or the echo of his father’s stories.

The lighthouse did not answer. It never had.

But as the beam swept across the blank horizon, he fancied he felt, deep beneath his boots, three soft knocks, not asking this time, but answering.

He opened the logbook and dipped his pen.

“2315 hours,” he wrote, hand steady. “Fog dense. Wind east-by-northeast. One man taken from the sea alive.”

He hesitated, then added, in smaller script below:

“Light continues to keep good watch. Not alone here.”

He sanded the ink, closed the book, and returned to the lantern room, where the lens turned and turned, tirelessly folding fire into guidance and giving it away to the dark.
